conversation.content:
Hello there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Patel, and I’m a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. I’m glad we have this time together to see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.

To do that, I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS, the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply a 10-question check-in that looks at mood, anxiety, and how life with your little one has felt over the past seven days. It’s not a test, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and our team, and we’ll go at your pace so you feel safe and supported. When we’re finished, we’ll talk about what the results might mean and any next steps that could be helpful.

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

I can still laugh, but it’s not quite the same. I’ll chuckle at little things the baby does, or something silly my husband says, yet it feels like I have to remind myself to enjoy it. Before she was born, everything seemed funnier—now it’s like the laughter is there, but it’s muted.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yes… most of the time I can still laugh. It doesn’t come as easily as it used to, but I do find things funny—especially when the baby makes those little faces. It just feels a bit forced sometimes, like I’m reminding myself to enjoy the moment rather than it happening naturally.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still look forward to some things—like taking the baby for walks or the rare coffee with a friend—but the excitement isn’t quite there. I’ll mark it on the calendar and think, “That’ll be nice,” yet when the time comes it feels kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions more than really enjoying it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time I do. If she’s fussy and I can’t settle her right away, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not feeding her properly or I missed some cue. Even little stuff, like spilling a bit of pumped milk, makes me feel like I’ve failed. I know in my head it’s not rational, but the thought still jumps in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll be sitting there with her sleeping peacefully and suddenly worry that she’s too quiet—so I’ll check her breathing three or four times. It only lasts a few minutes and I can calm myself, but it pops up out of nowhere, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky… more like a quick flutter of “what if something happens to her?” It’s not a full-on scare, just a little rush of worry that passes once I peek into the bassinet and see she’s okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… I do feel like that sometimes. Most days I manage to get through the feedings and the diapers and the house stuff, but every so often it all piles up—like when she won’t nap and the laundry’s staring at me—and I feel a wave of “I can’t keep up.” It passes if I take a breath and tackle one thing at a time, but in the moment it feels overwhelming.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad. I do wake up when she cries for feeds, but once she’s settled I can usually drift back off. Once or twice this week I lay there a little while staring at the ceiling, but I wouldn’t say I’m so unhappy that sleep won’t come—just normal new-mom broken nights.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I’ve felt that way off and on. Not all day, but there are stretches—especially toward evening—when I just feel kind of heavy and teary for no clear reason. It lifts after a while, but it’s definitely there more days than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… that’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was when she wouldn’t latch and I felt useless, and another night I just sat in the rocker with her asleep on my chest and the tears started rolling. It wasn’t all-day sobbing—just sudden, quiet crying that stopped after a few minutes.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… not at all. I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. Even on the weepy evenings, that idea has never crossed my mind.

You've shared that, over the past week, laughter and looking forward to things feel muted and "forced," and several evenings bring sudden heaviness or tears. While you care beautifully for your baby and can still find moments of joy, you often blame yourself when she fusses, find yourself repeatedly checking her breathing, and sometimes feel overwhelmed by everyday tasks. These changes are common in new motherhood, yet they seem to be taking a toll on your mood and confidence.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and anticipatory pleasure—events feel "flat" and routine—matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame occurs "a lot of the time" for routine infant-care difficulties, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intrusive worries about the baby's breathing that arise "out of nowhere" several times, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports periodic episodes of feeling overwhelmed that pass with effort, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, recurring sadness on most days, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 14 places you above the 13-point cutoff indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Key items contributing were <sym>blunted enjoyment</sym>, daily <sym>low mood</sym>, and frequent <sym>guilt</sym>. Your description of events feeling "flat" and crying "for no clear reason" aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> (≥5 symptoms present most days). Absence of self-harm thoughts is reassuring; nonetheless, the score mandates prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Continue regular check-ins with your midwife, health visitor, or obstetrician; request repeat EPDS in two weeks to track progress
3. Share screening results with trusted family or friends so they can support you and help monitor your mood
4. Prioritise rest: accept naps, split night duties with a partner when possible, and practise brief breathing exercises when feeling overwhelmed
5. Discuss evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, or <med>SSRIs</med> compatible with breastfeeding if recommended by your physician
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report via Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale–style interview 1–2 wks post-delivery.

Symptoms / Behaviours Identified  
- Persistent low mood: End-of-day “heavy/teary” episodes most days.  
- Anhedonia: Enjoyment blunted; activities feel “flat” or “forced.”  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame: Interprets routine infant care challenges as maternal failure.  
- Recurrent intrusive worries: Checks infant breathing multiple times daily.  
- Episodic overwhelm: “Wave of ‘I can’t keep up’” when tasks accumulate; improves with distraction.  
- Crying spells: Twice this week; situationally triggered (latch difficulty).  
- Mild sleep disruption: Initial insomnia after night feeds 1–2×/wk; denies inability to sleep due to mood.

Pattern  
Symptoms cluster in late afternoon/evening, remit with support or distraction; no functional impairment in basic infant care; no self-harm ideation.

Screening Significance  
Meets partial criteria for mild-moderate postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; does not meet threshold for major depressive episode (sleep/appetite largely intact, no suicidal thinking).

Risk Factors Present  
- Anhedonia + guilt  
- Recurrent tearfulness  
- Parenting-related anxiety

Safety  
Denies thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant; no protective concerns identified.

Plan  
Continue monitoring; consider formal EPDS scoring and follow-up visit within 2 wks or sooner if symptoms worsen or suicidal ideation emerges.
